rendered: The review does not actually recommend tens of nanometres. Its recommendation is thinner: it states that thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers[1]. The phrase about tens of nanometres describes what the literature usually reports, and the review says that thickness is hard to control with easily scalable processes. The reported coating thickness in literature, in most cases, is in the tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled by easily scalable processes.[2] The reasoning is that ZrO2 and similar oxides have extremely low lithium-ion diffusivity, so lithium transport through a thick layer is slow. The review modelled diffusion length over a range from 5nm to 50nm[3] and found that longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[4]. The review also notes that the lithium-ion diffusivity of most oxides and fluorides is low, particularly for ZrO2[5]. Its summary of scalable coatings says the same: they exhibit very low lithium-ion diffusivity[6] and their maximum thickness is usually recommended at about ∼10 nm[7]. A further reason is that inert coatings such as ZrO2 or Al2O3 may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases[8], which causes capacity fading, so a thin layer limits this side reaction as well.
